executive_view.headline: This dataset covers 3,000 orders across 12 months (Nov 2025 – Oct 2026), with revenue averaging $102.72 per order, three distinct customer segments, and a late-period dip worth watching.

paragraphs.text: The cleaned dataset contains 3,000 orders across 11 columns, with revenue ranging from $21.47 to $964.19 and a median of $100.33.
Segment A leads on average revenue ($121.29), followed by Segment B ($98.06) and Segment C ($78.88), while overall revenue slipped in the most recent month.
Data quality is largely sound after removing 25 duplicate rows, though the notes column is too empty to use and five revenue values fall far outside the usual range.

findings.text: Revenue varies meaningfully across the three segments: Segment A averages $121.29, Segment B $98.06, and Segment C $78.88 per order.

Overall revenue fell in Oct 2026 vs Sep 2026, and the decline was sharper for Segment B (-12.6%) than for the dataset as a whole (-2.8%) — these two signals point in the same direction but differ in magnitude.
Marketing spend and revenue move together across orders, suggesting the relationship is worth exploring further, though association does not confirm cause.
Discount and revenue show almost no association, so discount level alone does not appear to track with order revenue in this dataset — though this result is weak and uncertain.
Five revenue values fall far outside the usual range (above $260.65, with one reaching $964.19); they have been flagged but kept, and should be verified before any revenue totals are reported.

report.executive_summary: Overall, control converts better than treatment (60.0% vs. 40.0%), but this reverses within every department — a classic case of conflicting signals. Taken as a whole, control shows a mean conversion rate of 0.6 and treatment shows 0.4, suggesting control wins. However, when visitors are split by department, treatment outperforms control in both Easy (0.8 vs. 0.7) and Hard (0.3 vs. 0.2), meaning the overall result contradicts every within-department result. These two signals disagree and cannot both be taken at face value; the department mix assigned to each group is the most likely explanation and must be investigated before drawing a conclusion.

executive_view.headline: Overall, control converts better than treatment (60.0% vs. 40.0%), but this reverses within every department — a classic case of conflicting signals.

paragraphs.text: Taken as a whole, control shows a mean conversion rate of 0.6 and treatment shows 0.4, suggesting control wins.
However, when visitors are split by department, treatment outperforms control in both Easy (0.8 vs. 0.7) and Hard (0.3 vs. 0.2), meaning the overall result contradicts every within-department result.
These two signals disagree and cannot both be taken at face value; the department mix assigned to each group is the most likely explanation and must be investigated before drawing a conclusion.

findings.text: The overall conversion rate is 0.6 for control and 0.4 for treatment — but this overall comparison is misleading because the two groups appear to have different mixes of Easy and Hard department visitors.
Within the Easy department, treatment converts at 0.8 versus control at 0.7; within the Hard department, treatment converts at 0.3 versus control at 0.2 — treatment is ahead in both subgroups.

The Hard department has a much lower conversion rate (control 0.2, treatment 0.3) than the Easy department (control 0.7, treatment 0.8), so whichever group received more Hard visitors will look worse overall regardless of the treatment effect.
The overall mean conversion across all 2,000 visitors is 0.5, consistent with a roughly even split between converted and not-converted visitors.
